extracted.intended_audience: university technology transfer officers, university counsel, research administrators, and patent attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for university technology transfer and patenting practice: identifying and correcting inventorship, securing assignment/rights from researchers, and drafting patent disclosures (especially for unpredictable technologies such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventorship requires contemporaneous joint conception
rubrics_metrics.description: For a joint inventive collaboration to exist, the joint conception of the individuals involved must occur at or around the same time; contributions occurring fairly late in the project, especially after initial conception or after filing, are less likely to be inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: American Cyanamid (unauthorized use of university doctors' conception led to unjust enrichment judgment) and Oregon Health & Science University v. Vertex (later-discovered nonbinders discovered after filing did not create joint inventorship). Emphasize timing of conception as core to joint inventorship determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain contributions are non-inventive and do not create joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions that merely follow directions in reducing the invention to practice, make an obvious contribution or improvement, merely suggest a result, involve knowledge of only an insufficient portion of the invention, provide publicly available information, or contribute ideas that are part of the prior art will generally not be regarded as inventive contributions for joint inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even small communications that lead to joint conception can support joint inventorship, but the listed categories are generally excluded. Assess whether interaction led to joint conception, not merely execution or suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted inventor can be added post-grant only with stringent proof
rubrics_metrics.description: An omitted inventor can be added after the patent is granted, but this requires proof that the omission occurred without deceptive intent and clear and convincing evidence of the omitted inventor's contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the high burden, universities may be disadvantaged when attempting to add researchers post-grant; this underscores proactive inventorship practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, add the researcher as inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: As a practical rule, when there is doubt and a supportable basis exists, add the researcher as an inventor to avoid later problems with omitted inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding an inventor early generally provides a supportable basis for correcting inventorship later if necessary and reduces risk of post-grant disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain an assignment of title from inventors promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities should secure a transfer (assignment) of title in the invention rights from the inventor shortly before or after the patent is filed to ensure clear title for licensing and prosecution control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment is not required to obtain a patent but is important for licensing and for the university to direct the patent attorney. Example: Trustees of Boston University v. Beacon Laboratories — failure to secure rights from all inventors jeopardized a license and led to breach issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment agreements and patent policies can create binding assignment obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: A university's employment agreements or patent policies can obligate researchers (faculty, staff, and in many cases graduate students) to assign invention rights to the university.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Fenn v. Yale (written employment agreement/patent policy binding), Regents v. Univ. of New Mexico (annual agreement binding), Chou v. Univ. of Chicago and Van Voorhies (graduate students bound by patent policy). State law differences may affect outcomes; patent policies are a powerful tool even without separate employment contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment scope should be comprehensive and include worldwide rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment should provide the university with the right to pursue the patent throughout the world; any limitations on transfer may convert the assignment into a license or otherwise limit university rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft assignments to avoid geographic or other limiting language unless intended; confirm that the assignment conveys full ownership consistent with university goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include explicit right to sue for past infringement in assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: An often-overlooked right is the right of the university to sue for past infringement; this should be included in the assignment to permit recovery of damages that accrued prior to the execution of the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that a damages clause cannot be transferred separate from the patent itself. Although no particular language is required, the mere assignment of the patent does not always transfer the right to past damages—express inclusion is prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual agreement to assign future inventions may not automatically cover later-generation patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractual agreement to assign rights to future inventions does not necessarily create an assignment of those rights for subsequent or second-generation patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Van Voorhies II: assignment of original patents did not automatically apply to a second-generation patent; universities should carefully draft policies and agreements and consider whether patent policy language covers future inventions and later-generation patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities must diligently pursue ownership claims; statutes of limitations can bar relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay or failure to pursue assignment or ownership claims can result in losing the ability to enforce such obligations due to statutes of limitations or similar defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: University Patents Inc. v. Kligman — the court ruled the university's suit was barred by the statute of limitations despite an implied obligation. Prompt action is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities owe limited implied obligations to inventors; bad faith and abuse of discretion are actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: While patent policies/employment agreements can obligate assignment, universities may also owe implied obligations to inventors such as avoiding abuses of discretion and bad faith in dealing with inventors; absent bad faith, many decisions are within university discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signer v. University of California: jury found abuse of discretion where university divided revenue and gave inventors only a portion. Courts have held that inventors generally cannot assert university failure to accept invention within policy timeframes to regain ownership or obtain damages absent bad faith. Universities retain discretion over licensee selection, royalty terms, whether to license, or return rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description and enablement requirement: full, clear, concise, exact terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must contain 'a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art' to make and use the invention (the written description/enablement requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is especially significant for securing and enforcing broad claims in unpredictable technologies. Satisfying both possession (written description) and enablement is necessary; courts may apply a stringent standard for unpredictable arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpredictable technologies demand more disclosure and limit broad functional claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies considered 'unpredictable' (e.g., catalysis, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology) are subject to a more stringent written description/enablement standard, making it harder to obtain broad functionalized claims based solely on mechanism or function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents claiming genes/proteins functionally rather than structurally have fared poorly; courts often require more specific exemplification or working examples. Litigation often reveals that having only one or few working examples is risky in these fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts sometimes blur written description and enablement doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit opinions have at times blurred the distinction between written description (possession/adequate description) and enablement, complicating predictability of outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Enzo Biochem, Inc. v. Gen-Probe (initial invalidation for written description with reliance on enablement precedent, later reheard), Eli Lilly (adequate description feature emphasized). Expect overlapping analyses in biotech cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific sequence knowledge/possession is often required for DNA/protein claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have required adequate descriptive possession of nucleotide or amino acid sequences; mere reference to DNA encoding a protein may be insufficient without adequate structural description or sequence information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Wallach: knowledge of the complete amino acid sequence may establish possession of the DNA, but knowledge of only short fragments (e.g., 11 amino acids of a 185–192 amino acid protein) was insufficient. University of Rochester v. G.D. Searle: broad method claims lacking identification of specific drugs invalidated for failing written description/enabling disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplify extensively in patent disclosure for unpredictable arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent disclosures should exemplify as much as possible the scope of the claimed technology, including how to make and use it, and should define each term, component, and step in sufficient detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely exclusively on illustrative or prophetic examples without testing representative examples. Identify as many specific compounds as possible in pharmaceutical contexts; articulate operative limits and include tested working examples where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augment initial disclosure via continuations or provisional filings
rubrics_metrics.description: File continuation or provisional patent applications to include new working examples or new understandings about the technology to strengthen written description/enablement support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisionals are useful and relatively low-cost for multiple filings, but must still satisfy written description/enablement and should not be used as an excuse for sloppy filings (e.g., simply attaching a journal article). Treat each provisional as a substantive disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue broad method claims including methods for making/using genes or proteins
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, claim methods for making genes or proteins or using them (e.g., as probes, screening assays, DNA microchips) since method claims may sometimes survive written description/enablement scrutiny better than broad functional genus claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method claims for manufacture or use can offer alternative protection and may help prevent importation or use of products made by proprietary methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public presentations and disclosures can constitute a 'publication' or 'public use' affecting novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral or printed presentations at scientific meetings can be treated as printed publications or public uses and thus can start the one-year U.S. statutory bar to patentability (35 U.S.C. §102(b)) or affect absolute novelty countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors making a presentation a 'publication' include wide viewership including skilled persons, display duration, and lack of expectation that the information will not be copied. Oral presentations raise evidentiary issues about what was disclosed; be careful with timing of public talks and filings, and use confidentiality measures where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer written confidentiality obligations; be aware of foreign grace periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer having a written obligation of confidentiality when sharing inventions; Europe provides a six-month grace period to file a patent if confidentiality is breached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confidentiality agreements before disclosure. Remember that some jurisdictions (e.g., many European countries) have stricter absolute novelty standards and limited grace periods—plan filings accordingly.
